content: Diaphyseal fractures of the forearm in children are a frequent injury, often caused by falls. Treatment options for these fractures include non-surgical methods, such as manipulation followed by the application of a cast, and surgical methods, such as internal fixation using intramedullary nails or plates and screws. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects, including both benefits and harms, of surgical interventions compared to non-surgical interventions, as well as to compare different surgical techniques for fixing diaphyseal fractures of the radius and ulna in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register (as of March 2011), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (2011 Issue 1), MEDLINE (from 1948 to February 2011), EMBASE (from 1980 to the ninth week of 2011), as well as trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trials that compared surgical and non-surgical interventions, or different surgical techniques, for the treatment of diaphyseal forearm fractures in children. All authors of the review independently screened the search results to identify studies that met these criteria. Out of 163 citations initially identified, 15 studies were considered potentially eligible. However, 14 of these studies were excluded, and one study is still ongoing. As a result, no studies met the criteria for inclusion in this review. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence from randomised controlled trials to guide decisions on when surgery is necessary or which surgical technique is most effective for treating diaphyseal fractures of the radius, ulna, or both bones in children.
